claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial SDU rents.
A hard cap would transfer modest gains to incumbent tenants while shrinking stock for new households.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within existing tenancies but left initial rents untouched.
SDU stock grew from roughly 107,300 units in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025.
First-generation rent controls show consistent supply contraction, while second-generation controls show small or null effects.
The stable stock under the ordinance is what one would expect from a non-binding instrument.
The estimated long-run supply elasticity for SDU-type stock is 0.31 to 0.48.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
A modelled 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about HK$900 per month to incumbents.
A 15 percent cut would leave 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment.
Berlin's Mietendeckel suppressed initial-offer rents but triggered measurable supply contraction.
When Berlin's law was struck down, new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend line.
New York's 2019 tightening is associated with a fall in available stabilised listings.
Current SDU inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail of tenants.
Mr Chan fears landlords would rather convert cubicles back to storage than deal with regulated tenants.
The NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure.
The binding constraint is queue length and insecurity, not price.
The landlords' Association concedes it has no data on actual margins.
The alternative is to cap initial rent by reference to a published, indexed per-square-foot band.
The consultation document expected in 2026 appears to float a floor-standard plus rent band package.

cites.sentence: The archive's evidence converges on a single conclusion: a hard cap would transfer modest gains to incumbent tenants while shrinking the stock of units available to the very households the policy is meant to protect — new arrivals, single-parent families, and those waiting for public housing [D1p2].
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance was a second-generation instrument: it capped increases within an existing tenancy but left initial rents untouched [D1p3].
SDU stock did not contract; it grew from roughly 107,300 units in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025 [D2p1].

The academic literature distinguishes first-generation controls (hard caps on levels), which show consistent contraction, from second-generation controls (caps on increases), which show small or null effects [D6p2].
The estimated long-run supply elasticity for SDU-type stock is 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

In a modelled Hong Kong-like scenario, a 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about HK$900 per month to incumbents, against 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment — mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].

Berlin's Mietendeckel suppressed initial-offer rents but triggered measurable supply contraction as owners withheld or rerouted flats; when the law was struck down, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend line [D7p1][D7p2].

Berlin's Mietendeckel suppressed initial-offer rents but triggered measurable supply contraction as owners withheld or rerouted flats; when the law was struck down, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend line [D7p1][D7p2].

New York's rent stabilisation, a second-generation scheme light at first-rent, has seen only modest stock contraction — but its 2019 tightening is associated with a fall in available stabilised listings as owners shifted units to other uses [D8p1][D8p3].

New York's rent stabilisation, a second-generation scheme light at first-rent, has seen only modest stock contraction — but its 2019 tightening is associated with a fall in available stabilised listings as owners shifted units to other uses [D8p1][D8p3].

Current SDU inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].

More damning, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], or the newest arrivals — so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].

More damning, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], or the newest arrivals — so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].

Mr Chan is split: a hard cap would free maybe HK$800 a month, but he fears landlords would rather convert cubicles back to storage than deal with regulated tenants — and he has seen two units on his floor emptied and locked for a year [D3p2].
Asked what would help most, he does not name rent; he names the waiting list [D3p3].
The NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].

The landlords' threat of exit should be treated with caution — the Association concedes it has no data on actual margins, and its compliance-cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3].
Mrs Wong's observation that units are landlords' pension and they would not leave is plausible [D4p2].
But even a modest, credible exit risk is enough to make a hard cap the wrong instrument when the elasticity literature points to contraction [D6p1].
The alternative is already on the table: cap initial rent by reference to a published, indexed per-square-foot band, defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation [D9p2].
Pair this with tenure security — written agreements, notice periods, and enforcement focused on conditions rather than price [D11p2].
The consultation document expected in 2026 appears to float exactly this "floor-standard + rent band" package [D12p1].
